slides.title: Searching a sorted list
slides.text: Searching a sorted list - Linear search: up to n checks - Sorted order lets us skip most of them

slides.title: The idea
slides.text: The idea - Look at the middle element - Too small? Discard the left half - Too big? Discard the right half - Repeat on what is left

slides.title: Example: find 23
slides.text: Example: find 23 [ 2 5 8 12 16 23 38 56 72 91 ] mid = 16 -> go right mid = 56 -> go left mid = 23 -> found

slides.title: Why about log2 n steps
slides.text: Why about log2 n steps n -> n/2 -> n/4 -> ... -> 1 1,000,000 items: about 20 steps

slides.title: Off-by-one traps
slides.text: Off-by-one traps while lo <= hi: mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2

slides.title: Summary
slides.text: Summary - Sorted input + halving = O(log n) - Get the loop bounds right

segments.raw_text: OK, um, so today is binary search, which you've probably, uh, seen before, but we're going to do it properly.
segments.speaker: Lecturer

segments.raw_text: So if a list isn't sorted, you've got no choice, you check every element. That's up to n checks. But if it is sorted, you know, the order itself tells you where things can't be.
segments.speaker: Lecturer

segments.raw_text: So you get to skip most of them.
segments.speaker: Lecturer

segments.raw_text: The idea is dead simple. Look at the middle. If it's too small, everything to the left is too small as well, throw it away.
segments.speaker: Lecturer

segments.raw_text: If it's too big, throw away the right half. Then just do the same thing on whatever's left.
segments.speaker: Lecturer

segments.raw_text: Let's find twenty three. Middle is sixteen, too small, so we go right. Now the middle is fifty six, too big, go left. And the middle of what's left is twenty three.
segments.speaker: Lecturer

segments.raw_text: Found it in three looks instead of six.
segments.speaker: Lecturer

segments.raw_text: Why is it log n? Every step halves what's left. n, then n over two, n over four, until there's one thing left. How many halvings to get from a million to one?
segments.speaker: Lecturer

segments.raw_text: About twenty. Twenty looks for a million items. That's the whole point.
segments.speaker: Lecturer

segments.raw_text: Now, this is where everyone gets it wrong. It's lo less than or equal to hi, not less than, or you miss the last element.
segments.speaker: Lecturer

segments.raw_text: And write mid as lo plus hi minus lo over two. In some languages lo plus hi can overflow, and that bug sat in real libraries for years.
segments.speaker: Lecturer

segments.raw_text: Oh, before I forget, assignment one. It's due Friday of week four at five pm, it's worth fifteen percent, and you submit it on the course website, not by email.
segments.speaker: Lecturer
